title: Hard Times and What to Hold Onto
overview: Paul warns Timothy about people who look religious but live selfishly and mislead others, and urges him to hold to what he learned from Paul's example and from Scripture.

parts.label: Hard times coming (vv. 1-5)
parts.note: Paul lists traits like greed, pride and cruelty, ending with people who keep religion's outward look but reject the power that should change them (v. 5). Christians differ on whether 'the last days' means the whole age since Jesus or a final stretch before his return, but Paul's order to avoid such people suggests he saw them around him already.

parts.label: Teachers who target households (vv. 6-7)
parts.note: These teachers slip into homes and win over women whom Paul describes with a belittling word ('gullible' in the NIV, 'silly' in the ASV) as weighed down by guilt and always chasing new ideas without reaching the truth. Scholars often link this to a specific problem in Timothy's church, and readers differ on how far the harsh wording reflects the attitudes of its time.

parts.label: Like Pharaoh's magicians (vv. 8-9)
parts.note: Exodus 7 does not name the Egyptian magicians who copied Moses' signs, but later Jewish tradition called them Jannes and Jambres. Paul says these teachers will fail the same way, with their foolishness plain for everyone to see.

parts.label: Paul's life as a model (vv. 10-13)
parts.note: Timothy knew how Paul taught and lived, and the attacks he faced in Antioch, Iconium and Lystra, towns in Timothy's home region where Paul was driven out and, at Lystra, stoned (Acts 13 and 14). Paul says anyone who truly wants to live for Jesus will face opposition, while deceivers sink deeper into deceiving others and being deceived themselves.

parts.label: Hold on to what you learned (vv. 14-15)
parts.note: Paul urges Timothy to trust what he learned from people he knew well, likely including his mother and grandmother (1:5). The Scriptures he knew from infancy were the Jewish Scriptures, which Christians call the Old Testament, and Paul says they lead to rescue through trusting Christ Jesus.

parts.label: What Scripture is for (vv. 16-17)
parts.note: Paul uses a rare Greek word saying Scripture comes from God's breath, which the NIV renders 'God-breathed' and the ASV 'inspired of God', and he says it equips a person to teach, correct and live rightly. The two translations also build the sentence differently, since the NIV says all Scripture is inspired and useful while the ASV says every inspired scripture is also useful, which a few read as a narrower claim.

disagreement: Protestant Christians often read verses 16 and 17 as showing that Scripture alone is the final authority for faith, while Catholic and Orthodox Christians agree Scripture is inspired but hold that these verses do not rule out the church's tradition alongside it.
think: When you decide whether to trust what someone teaches you, how much does it matter that you have seen how they actually live?
